name: Code review
title: Code review: {{repo}} PR {{number}} ({{short_title}})
description:
Code review of {{repo}} PR #{{number}} ({{ticket}}, "{{title}}", {{files}} files, +{{added}} -{{removed}}, {{draft}}): {{pr}}

How to review (use {{review_skill}}):
Load the review skill first, before the steps below. Only the user can start it, so it is hidden from your Skill tool and missing from your skill list: that is expected, not a problem, so do not report it or postpone it. Read its SKILL.md now (installPath of its plugin in ~/.claude/plugins/installed_plugins.json, then skills/<name>/SKILL.md), follow it with the pull request link as its argument, and say in one line which file you loaded. Do not post to GitHub unless I ask. Only if no such file exists, say so and ask me before using another skill.
0. Which code is reviewed (read this first): this session runs in the barad-dur folder, NOT in the repo of the pull request. A bare PR number or "the current diff" would be read against barad-dur itself, which is wrong. Always target the pull request by its full link ({{pr}}), and before reviewing confirm the run is about {{repo}} #{{number}} (the title and the files must match the PR above). If the skill cannot take a link, or it ends up reviewing uncommitted changes of this workspace, stop and tell me: never report a review of this workspace as a review of the PR. If it cannot be done, review by hand from `gh pr diff` and `gh pr view` (add --repo <org>/{{repo}}) and the code on fresh origin/main.
1. Read the PR diff and the ticket. Read the repo on fresh origin/main with `git -C <path to the repo's own folder> fetch` and then git show / git grep, without switching branches and without making any copy.
2. Bugs and regressions: look for new bugs or issues, and for behavior that changes for existing callers.
3. Scope: check the PR does only what the ticket asks. List anything extra, and anything the ticket asks for that is missing.
4. Cross-service impact: check whether the change affects other services (callers, events, shared contracts or data). Use the code and the logs as evidence.
5. Risk analysis: give a risk level with a level of confidence, and say which parts rest on code evidence and which on log evidence.
6. Recommendation: end with a clear verdict on whether to approve or not, with the reasons.
7. Comments: write every review comment needed, including inline ones (file and line), in the Findings tab. Do not post anything to GitHub unless I ask.
